Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you’re jumping in from the very beginning, that’s exactly the right place to start.

When you shop with Heirloom, these are the main “big decisions,” in simple terms:

Where the rose will live
In the ground: Great if you have a garden bed with at least 6 hours of sun (this is called “full sun”).
In a pot: Works well on patios or decks. Use a large container (about 10 gallons) with good-quality potting soil. All of our roses come in 1-gallon containers with soil; you’ll transplant them into the ground or a bigger pot.
How much sun the spot gets
Full sun: 6 or more hours of direct sun per day. Most roses love this.
Partial shade: 4 or more hours of sun per day; some roses will still do well here. This helps you decide where you can successfully plant, so the rose has enough energy to bloom.
Type and size of rose On the site under “Shop All Roses,” you’ll see types:
Shrub/bush roses: Rounded shape, great for most gardens.
Climbing roses: Long canes you tie to an arch, fence, or trellis.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low and spreading, good for covering areas. Sizes on our pages are in feet, not inches, so you know how tall and wide the plant will get.
Look and fragrance You can filter by:
Color (pink, red, yellow, apricot, etc.)
Fragrance (light, strong, or none)
Bloom style (big classic blooms, clusters of smaller flowers, etc.) This is the “fun” part: picking what you want it to look and smell like.

Your climate (hardiness zone) At the top of the website you can choose your hardiness zone. That helps show roses that are suited to your weather so they have the best chance to thrive.

Extras (optional)

Soil amendments and fertilizers (things that help the soil and feed the rose)
Garden markers (metal tags or stakes with the rose’s name engraved) These are nice add-ons but not required to get started.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You really don’t need a ton to get started, but a few things can make it easier and set your first rose up for success.

The basics (must-haves)
A sunny spot: Ideally full sun (6+ hours of direct sun) or at least partial shade (4+ hours).
Good-quality soil: Well-draining garden soil or potting soil if you’re using a container.
A larger container (if potting): About 10 gallons for long-term growth.
Water source nearby: So you can water deeply and regularly.
Helpful soil amendments (optional but recommended) These improve the soil your rose grows in:
Bone meal: Supports strong root development when planting.
Cow manure: Adds long-lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost: Helps aerate (loosen) the soil and can also be used on top as a protective layer around the roots.
Worm castings: Gently feed the plant and improve soil structure.

You can mix these into the planting area or potting soil before planting. They’re not required, but they give beginners a nice safety net.

Fertilizer (this is important) Roses are hungry plants, so fertilizing really matters:
We offer fertilizers like OmniMeal, Founders Fish Fertilizer, and Boost & Bloom, but you can use any good rose fertilizer you like.
For the first year, a liquid fertilizer is usually easiest for beginners because it’s simple to apply when you water.
A quick how-to guide If you haven’t seen it yet, this walkthrough is very beginner friendly:
Planting step-by-step: Planting Roses
General how-to for new growers: How to Start Growing Roses – No Experience Needed

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

I’ll walk you through using your very first rose correctly from day one.

I’ll explain:

How to plant your new rose the first time

How to use any extras (amendments/fertilizer) without overdoing it

Using your new rose properly the first time (planting)

This is the basic, beginner-friendly way to start:

Timing

Plant after your last spring frost, or at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
Roses must live outdoors (in the ground or in a pot). Keeping them indoors long-term will cause problems and also voids our guarantee.

Take it out of the shipping container

Your rose arrives as an own-root rose in a 1‑gallon container with soil and trimmed canes (often without leaves yet, which is normal).
Gently squeeze or tap the sides of the pot and slide the whole root ball out. Do not pull hard on the stems.

Choose the spot or pot

Sun: Aim for full sun (about 6+ hours of direct sun). Partial shade (around 4+ hours) can work for some spots, but more sun usually means more blooms.
Ground planting: Dig a hole about 2 ft wide and deep enough that the top of the existing soil on the root ball will sit level with the surrounding soil.
Container planting: Use a larger pot (about 10–15 gallons) with drainage holes and good-quality potting soil.

Planting the rose

Place the rose in the center of the hole or pot.
Make sure the top of the existing root ball is level with the surrounding soil, not buried deeper.
Backfill around it with soil, gently pressing to remove air pockets but not stomping hard.

Watering the first time

Water slowly and deeply right after planting until the soil is thoroughly moist.
Let the water soak in, then water a bit more. This helps settle the soil around the roots.
How to use “extras” the first time (without overdoing it)

You do not have to use every product. These are simple, safe ways to start:

A) Soil amendments at planting (optional, but helpful) You can mix any of these into the planting area or potting soil:

Bone meal: Mix a small amount into the planting soil to support root growth.
Cow manure (aged/composted): Mix into the soil you backfill with; it slowly feeds the plant.
Mint compost: Mix some into the soil for better texture, and you can also spread a thin layer on top as mulch to protect roots.
Worm castings: Mix a small handful or two into the planting soil for gentle nutrients.

Keep it light and well mixed; the planting hole should still mostly be your regular soil or potting soil, not pure amendments.

B) Fertilizer the first time For your very first season, simple is best:

Use a gentle or liquid fertilizer rather than a strong granular one right at planting.
Apply according to the label, usually after the rose has been in the ground for a little bit and is starting to grow.
Water after fertilizing so it reaches the roots.
